planting.note: Set out container-grown offsets after all frost danger in gritty, mineral soil in full sun, where intense light helps bring out the reddish leaf color.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, gritty mineral soil in full sun, since this Richtersveld native needs intense heat and light to thrive and performs poorly in cool, overcast conditions. Clustering upright stems carry triangular, backward-curving gray-green leaves that flush deep red to maroon when grown lean and dry, with tubular red, yellow, or bicolor flowers opening in summer. It is a slow grower and sensitive to overwatering, especially in summer, so let the soil dry thoroughly between waterings and keep it nearly dry in winter. Protect from any frost and give it the hottest, brightest spot available in the garden or a bright container position where winters are cold.

common_name: Dwarf Carpet of Stars (Nana Vygie Ice Plant Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant rooted plugs or divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; spacing closer together speeds full lawn-substitute coverage.

directions: Plant divisions or plugs in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this dwarf selection of a Little Karoo and Western Cape vygie forms a dense, flat mat under two inches tall, with tiny three-angled green leaves held in neat crisscrossed pairs along thin reddish stems. Small white-centered pink flowers appear in spring and again in fall, covering the mat in color without ever needing mowing. It tolerates foot traffic better than most succulents and is used as a low-water lawn substitute, taking winter lows into the low twenties Fahrenheit once established. Water occasionally during the hottest, driest stretches of summer to keep the mat dense, but avoid heavy irrigation, which encourages rot and weed competition.
sources: SANBI Red List of South African Plants

common_name: Bushman's Candle (Pink Candle Bush, Karoo Waxy-Stemmed Succulent)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after frost danger has passed into extremely well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; the waxy stem coating is easily damaged by handling, so transplant with care.

directions: Grow in lean, extremely well-drained, gritty soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky flats and quartz patches of its Nama Karoo and Namaqualand home. This low, many-branched shrublet coats its thin, spine-tipped stems in a thick, flammable wax that once served as emergency tinder for Khoisan fire-starting, giving rise to its common name. Small heart-shaped leaves emerge in the spine axils, and pink-to-orange, five-petaled flowers open from the stem tips mainly in late spring into early summer. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and prone to stem rot if kept wet or cold, so withhold water almost entirely through winter and protect it from any frost.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Sow seed in early fall as temperatures start to drop, following its winter-rainfall native cycle; keep the tuber completely dry during its summer dormancy.

directions: Grow in a very gritty, mineral potting medium or raised bed in full sun, replicating the winter-wet, summer-dry cycle of its narrow west-coast Namaqualand to Richtersveld range. A fat, woody underground tuber sends up a low rosette of grayish, finely divided leaves each fall, followed in late winter into spring by a single tall stalk topped with a dense cluster of twenty or more small flowers ranging from deep red-purple to pale mauve or near-white. After flowering the foliage dies back and the tuber must be kept bone dry through the hot summer months to avoid rot. Repot or top-dress with fresh gritty soil during the late-summer dormant season rather than while the plant is actively growing.

planting.note: Start seed or set out young container-grown plants after all frost danger in extremely well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; container culture in a shallow pot encourages the thick caudex to bulk up like a bonsai.

directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, lean soil in full sun, giving the swollen, gnarled succulent trunk room to expand with age. Exfoliating, papery white bark peels back to reveal blue-green photosynthetic tissue beneath, and tiny, soft, pinnately divided leaves emerge each spring before dropping in summer drought or winter cold. Small cream-to-pink flowers appear from late spring into early fall depending on moisture. In the ground it slowly becomes a small gnarled tree, while container specimens stay dwarfed and bonsai-like for decades; water lightly in summer and more generously in winter, following its natural winter-growing cycle, and protect from any hard freeze, since temperatures below the mid-20s Fahrenheit can kill the plant.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, sharply drained soil on a sunny slope or bluff; established plants resent summer irrigation and prefer to be left dry.

directions: Plant on a sunny, well-drained slope or bluff in lean soil, matching the coastal sage scrub and maritime succulent scrub habitat this species occupies from San Diego County south through Baja California and Isla Guadalupe. Thick gray-green succulent stems hold small rounded leaves that drop in drought, and clusters of inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear quickly after any rain, often repeating several times a year. It stands erect in sheltered sites but grows low and sprawling where exposed to constant onshore wind, so site and prune according to the look desired. Give it excellent drainage and minimal summer water once established, since this milky-sapped species is adapted to long dry spells and rots readily in heavy, poorly drained soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; site away from paths, since mature leaves end in sharp points.

directions: Plant in rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Baja California peninsula endemic forms a thick, often branching trunk topped with dense rosettes of stiff, narrow, blue-green leaves edged with fine teeth. It grows slowly but steadily into a small, picturesque tree, eventually producing tall spikes of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant and need almost no supplemental water, while young plants benefit from occasional deep watering to speed trunk formation. It tolerates brief light frost once mature but is best reserved for frost-free to nearly frost-free gardens, and like other tree yuccas it is slow enough from seed that most garden specimens start as nursery-grown plants.
sources: San Diego Natural History Museum Field Guide (Ocean Oasis)

common_name: Cedros Island Agave (Baja Island Blue Agave)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun near the coast; this island species prefers a mild, Mediterranean-type climate over hot interior heat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; native to Cedros, Natividad, and San Benito Islands off central Baja California, this agave forms broad, striking blue-gray rosettes of fleshy leaves armed with large dark marginal teeth and a long terminal spine. It clusters over time into handsome multi-headed groups and tolerates drought and salt-laden coastal air well, performing best in the mild, fog-influenced conditions of its island origin rather than scorching desert heat. After roughly two decades of growth, a tall stalk of yellow flowers emerges and the flowering rosette dies, but offsets left behind continue the clump. Avoid summer overwatering, since it is adapted to a winter-rainfall cycle and rots in constantly wet soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in extremely well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; give winter protection in any climate that sees more than light, brief frost.

directions: Plant in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; this compact subspecies of Agave cerulata from the central Baja California peninsula forms short-stemmed, broad-leaved rosettes with wider, less numerous leaves than the typical clustering form, giving it a slightly bulkier, more solitary appearance. Mature rosettes send up a very tall, candelabra-like flower stalk bearing light yellow blooms after many years of slow growth, after which the parent rosette dies back. It handles heat and long dry spells with ease but is more cold-sensitive than many landscape agaves, so it suits warm coastal and desert gardens better than regions with regular hard freezes. Keep soil on the dry side through winter to prevent crown rot.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Start seed indoors or set out young container-grown plants after frost danger in sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun; this slow-growing island endemic is well suited to long-term container culture.

directions: Grow in sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun; native to Cedros Island off Baja California, this barrel cactus carries thirteen to twenty-two ribs densely armed with curved, showy spines that emerge golden-yellow and gray with age, giving the species its name. It usually grows as a solitary barrel for many years before occasionally clustering with age, and produces yellow, gold, orange, or peach-toned flowers in a ring near the crown during summer. Its dense spine coat allows it to take full sun even in hot inland gardens, but it is a notably slow grower, so patience and consistently sharp drainage matter more than frequent feeding or watering. Keep it dry and protected from frost over winter.

planting.note: Start seed indoors or set out young container-grown plants after frost danger in sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun; give it a permanent, open site with room to grow, since mature specimens become massive.

directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun with plenty of open room, since this is the tallest-growing cactus species in the world and the dominant giant columnar cactus of the Sonoran Desert and Baja California's Vizcaino desert. A thick central trunk branches into several to many upright, ribbed, gray-green columns bearing clusters of stout spines, and night-blooming white to pale pink flowers open near the stem tips in late spring, pollinated by bats and later producing edible fruit. Growth is very slow for the first years and young plants need occasional summer watering while establishing, but mature specimens are extremely drought tolerant and can be damaged by overwatering or heavy, poorly drained soil. It tolerates brief light frost but is best grown in reliably warm, frost-free to nearly frost-free gardens.
sources: Palm Springs Living Desert reference collection
